newsitem.title: USA: Hewlett-Packard cuts prices on business PCs.
newsitem.headline: Hewlett-Packard cuts prices on business PCs.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp., aiming to cement its position as the world's largest personal computer maker, said Monday it was cutting prices up to 17 percent on desktop computers and by 27 percent on notebooks aimed at businesses.
Separately, Hewlett-Packard Co. said it also cut prices on some PCs aimed at small businesses.

"Compaq expects this action to help enable it to continue the success we had last year as the No. 1 market share leader for the third consecutive year," said James Schraith, vice president and general manager of Compaq North America.
Houston-based Compaq said its Deskpro 2000 machine with a Pentium 133 megahertz processor and 1.2 gigabyte hard drive was cut to $1,150 from $1,360.
The more powerful 2500 model with a 166 MHz chip and 2.5 GB hard drive was reduced to $1,465 from $1,765, a Compaq spokesman said.
Prices for the desktop models do not include monitors, some of which were also reduced in price.
The Deskpro 4000, aimed at businesses that want to link machines into networks, now starts at $1,290, down from $1,510, Compaq said. The machine has a 133 MHz Pentium chip and 1 GB hard drive.
The Deskpro 6000, cut to $1,980 from $2,300, has a 166 MHz Pentium processor, 1 GB hard drive and 16 MB of memory.
Compaq also cut prices on its LTE and Armada notebook computers.
Compaq said the Armada 4110 now starts at $1,599, compared with $2,199, and the LTE 5400 was cut to $5,199 from $5,599.
The Armada 4110 weighs 5.1 pounds, has a colour display, 8 megabytes of memory and an 810 MB hard drive. The LTE 5400 offers 2.1 GB hard drive, 32 MB of memory and a 150 MHz Pentium chip.
In addition, Compaq cut prices by up to 11 percent on its ProLiant 5000 server, a machine that links computers into networks for businesses and other users.
Separately, Hewlett-Packard Co. said it cut prices up to 14 percent on its Vectra 500 PCs.
The price cuts would bring the retail price of the entry-level HP Vectra 520 model as low as $1,108 in the United States and Canada, HP said.
The Palo Alto, Calif.-based computer maker said the machines were aimed at businesses without management information system staff.
The Vectra 520 desktop has a 133 MHz Pentium chip, 12 MB of memory and a 1.2 GB hard drive. Other more powerful models were also reduced, HP said.
